definition: Summarize means to restate something in a much shorter form, keeping only the main points and letting the details fall away.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word summarize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know summarize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Asked about the four-hour hearing, the aide summarized it in a single line: the vote will be close, and it will be Tuesday.
Recap is lighter than summarize: a recap quickly runs back over what just happened for someone catching up, while to summarize is the fuller work of pulling every main point out of the whole.
Distill goes further than summarize: summarizing keeps all of the main points, while distilling boils the material down to its single purest idea and lets even minor points go.

Condense means to press something into less space while keeping all of its essential content — a condensed book keeps every chapter, just tighter. Summarize goes further: you keep only the main points and deliberately let the details fall away.

Recap means to run back quickly over what has already been said or happened, usually right afterward and for someone catching up — a coach recaps the first half at halftime. Summarize is the broader act of reducing any material to its main points, spoken or written, at any distance from the original.

Paraphrase means to restate someone's words in your own words at about the same length and level of detail — it changes the wording, not the amount. Summarize changes the amount: a summary is drastically shorter than what it restates.

Summarize means to restate something in a much shorter form, keeping only the main points and letting the details fall away.
The new ranger noticed that nobody read the forty pages of trail regulations posted in the trailhead kiosk.
Over the winter she summarized them onto a single carved sign — stay on the marked path, pack out what you pack in, camp only below the tree line — and rule-breaking fell by half before summer.
Forty pages became three essentials.
Cutting a long text down to the few points that matter most, and letting everything else go, is exactly what it means to summarize.
neutral — the everyday workhorse
Summarize is the plain, everyday verb for shrinking material to its main points, equally at home in a classroom and a boardroom.
Keep it apart from paraphrase, which changes the wording but not the amount, and from condense, which squeezes everything tighter without discarding anything.
If you kept only what matters most, you summarized.
The thing you produce is a summary.

Every Friday, ranger Elena Cruz files the week's trail report: forty pages of sensor logs, visitor counts, and maintenance notes.
Almost no one at headquarters reads it.
What they read is the paragraph she writes last.

In it she summarizes the week — three sentences naming the washed-out footbridge, the bear sighting near the north loop, and the record Saturday crowds — and lets the other thirty-nine pages go unmentioned.
A new supervisor once asked her to include everything important.
'Everything important is in the paragraph,' she answered.
'Everything else is in the forty pages.' The budget office, she has noticed, quotes only the paragraph.
